thesis.question: Why does AI adoption produce faster individuals without consistently producing faster or cheaper delivery?
thesis.claim: AI can improve or worsen task speed and correctness while increasing downstream review and maintenance work, so teams should measure those effects and address delivery bottlenecks before scaling generation.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that wider access to a more capable coding model will translate individual speed gains into broadly similar delivery and cost gains across teams.
thesis.so_what: Leaders need measured task and system outcomes to decide where to invest; otherwise they can expand review queues and maintenance bills while celebrating faster generation.
thesis.how_why: Capability varies across tasks, ownership costs sit downstream of generation, and a faster non-bottleneck cannot increase throughput beyond the stage that limits the delivery chain.

supporting_claims.claim: The amplifier image is useful for asking how context changes an AI outcome, but it is not a universal arithmetic law.
Task studies show why actual time, output, and correctness must be measured separately from the feeling of speed.
Faster generation can add ownership and coordination work at the stages that constrain delivery.
Standards and organizational foundations shape whether more generation becomes reliable work.
Teams should strengthen inputs and measure the limiting stages before expanding AI use.

role.contribution: Explains why adding generation to the surrounding system can increase strain unless teams address its inputs and limiting stages.

flow.rationale: The opening challenges automatic acceleration. The model and its limits come before the studies so readers do not mistake a mnemonic for a law. Measured task variation precedes lifecycle cost; cost leads directly to the delivery bottleneck, then the individual/team gap it explains. Quality and organizational foundations answer what makes greater output usable before the Monday moves and team questions apply it. The closing combines input quality with stage choice and hands the already named understanding burden to the next essay. Delaying limits would let readers interpret the differing study measures as one multiplier; separating cost from bottlenecks would hide where the relocated work lands; leaving questions after references would interrupt the final synthesis and lose their unit alignment.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The familiar promise that buying AI tools makes all work faster is the assumption this essay tests.

evidence.what:
> **KEY POINTS:**
>
> * **"Accelerator" is the wrong word.** An accelerator only adds speed, always in the same direction. AI doesn't add — it *multiplies*. It takes whatever you already have and makes it bigger: a skill, a process, a codebase, a goal.
> * **A multiplier keeps the sign of its input.** Point AI at strength and it compounds the strength. Point it at a mess — a brittle process, a confused goal, no standards — and it compounds the mess, faster and more expensively. The same tool that makes one developer 39% faster makes another, on a codebase he knows by heart, measurably *slower*.
> * **So the leverage is never in the AI — it is in what, and which part, you amplify.** An amplifier acts on one part, not the whole: speed up the fast stage of an unbalanced system and you just jam the bottleneck behind it. That is why individuals feel faster while their teams often don't. The durable work isn't a bigger multiplier; it's fixing the input and widening the slowest part.
evidence.shows: The unchanged three-bullet KEY POINTS callout gives the author's shorthand for variable outcomes, input quality, and downstream constraints; the prose must bound that shorthand as a metaphor.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The claim that AI makes work faster is true in some measured settings and false in others.
The METR result shows why a felt speedup cannot substitute for measuring task completion.

evidence.what: Mid-2025 randomized controlled trial: sixteen experienced open-source developers on their own large, mature repositories were 19% slower with AI while estimating about 20% faster.
evidence.shows: The measured result and the developers' perception had opposite directions in this setting; preserve all figures and qualifications.
evidence.source: METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity; existing July 2025 reference.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that AI makes work faster is true in some measured settings and false in others.
transition_in.introduces: The METR result shows why a felt speedup cannot substitute for measuring task completion.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The cited Copilot field experiments show that benefits can differ between junior and senior developers.

evidence.what: GitHub Copilot field experiments at Microsoft and Accenture: juniors and recent hires completed 27–39% more tasks; the most senior developers gained on the order of 8–13%.
evidence.shows: These task-output results illustrate different gains in their studied settings; comparison with METR is not a common-tool controlled comparison. Explain that positive gain was an assumption of the opening arithmetic, while the sign of the measured effect compares work with and without AI; expertise alone does not predict benefit because task/tool fit matters.
evidence.source: Copilot field experiments; existing MIT Sloan write-up.

transition_in.carries_over: The METR result shows why a felt speedup cannot substitute for measuring task completion.
transition_in.introduces: The cited Copilot field experiments show that benefits can differ between junior and senior developers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The jagged frontier describes task-dependent competence, including cases where AI lowers correctness.

evidence.what: Harvard and Boston Consulting Group, 2023: on eighteen inside-frontier tasks, AI users completed 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, at higher quality; on an outside-frontier task they were 19% less likely to reach the correct answer.
evidence.shows: Task fit changes the result; task count, completion time, and correctness remain distinct outcomes.
evidence.source: Dell'Acqua et al., Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier (2023); existing linked reference.

evidence.what: Preserve the accelerator-story / studies table and every percentage.
evidence.shows: The contrasts oppose uniform gains, expert advantage, perceived speed as measurement, and tool-only explanations; read the percentages with their preceding outcome labels. Before the table, distinguish elapsed time, completed tasks, and correctness as separate measures from separate studies.

evidence.what: Figure 2: speed-spectrum.jpeg; preserve image, alt text, and caption exactly.
evidence.shows: The spectrum illustrates variability qualitatively; the studies do not share a single performance measure or experimental setting. Establish before the visual that its range is a schematic of direction, not a quantitative ranking on one speed scale.

transition_in.carries_over: The cited Copilot field experiments show that benefits can differ between junior and senior developers.
transition_in.introduces: The jagged frontier describes task-dependent competence, including cases where AI lowers correctness.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The practical response to varied study outcomes is to measure the particular user-task combination rather than infer speed from the tool or the feeling.

evidence.what: Apply the distinction already introduced before the comparison: elapsed time, completed tasks, and correctness require task-specific measurement.

flow.rationale: Start with the speed promise, show a perception-reversing slowdown, contrast reported gains, then explain task fit and draw a measurement rule. Putting the rule first would hide the reason perception alone is unreliable; treating the studies as one scale would defeat the bounded model.

Historical Structure record retained for traceability; the moves explicitly decided above supersede only its order: House style (KEY POINTS block → MADR-ish body → contrast tables → Monday moves →
Closing → To Probe Further → Questions). Section order:

1. **The Wrong Word** — the accelerator framing and why it misleads; introduce
   amplifier.
2. **A Multiplier, Not an Adder** — the mechanism: `gain × input`, sign
   preserved; lineage (Engelbart's "intelligence amplification"; Jobs' "bicycle
   for the mind").
3. **It Amplifies Speed (in Both Directions)** — METR −19% (and the +20%
   perception gap); Copilot juniors +27–39% vs seniors +8–13%; BCG/Harvard
   jagged frontier (+12.2% inside, −19% correct outside).
4. **It Amplifies Cost** — cheap to generate, expensive to own; the cost-structure
   data.
5. **It Amplifies the Bottleneck (Friction in an Unbalanced System)** — a system
   is series-connected; amplify one part of an unbalanced system and the strain
   moves to the part you didn't (review, integration, fragile legacy), often
   making it worse. Theory of Constraints; CircleCI feature-branch +59% while
   median main-branch throughput fell; the legacy-gets-less-stable dynamic.
6. **Why Your Team Didn't Get Faster (Even Though You Did)** — individual gains
   real but absorbed at the bottleneck and lost to coordination friction; DORA
   2024 (individuals felt more productive; system throughput/stability down);
   Brooks-style communication overhead as everyone moves at different speeds.
7. **It Amplifies Quality — and Slop** — standards/guardrails set the sign; tie to
   the reactor "plant."
8. **It Amplifies Organizations** — DORA amplifier finding, seven profiles, the
   foundational capabilities that decide the sign.
9. **Where the Metaphor Breaks** — holds/breaks contrast table.
10. **What to Do on Monday** — move / what-it-looks-like / what-it-buys table
    (now includes "amplify the bottleneck, not the fast part").
11. **Closing Thought** — the multiplier acts on the number you give it; the work
    is the number.

Framed the whole post on the **multiplier vs. adder** distinction rather than just "amplifier sounds nicer than accelerator." Chosen because the sign-preservation (`gain × input`, input can be negative) is what makes the claim falsifiable and practical, not just rhetorical. Rejected: a looser "AI amplifies everything" framing with no mechanism.

Organized the body around **four axes** (speed, cost, quality, organization), each a cliché the post refuses with data. Rejected: a single software-delivery focus (too narrow) and a pure org/society essay (too far from the strongest evidence, which is software-delivery-centric).

Added a **systems/friction** strand (two new sections: the bottleneck, and the individual-vs-team gap) at the author's request. Chosen because it sharpens the thesis from "amplifying a negative is bad" to the more practical "amplifying *one part of an unbalanced system* relocates and worsens the strain" — grounded in the Theory of Constraints rather than asserted. Placed right after Cost (the bottleneck is where relocated cost lands) and before Quality/Organization. Rejected: folding it into the Organizations section (too cramped; the constraint point and the coordination point each deserve their own beat) and adding it as a single section (the *system has a bottleneck* and *teams don't get the individual gain* are distinct claims with distinct evidence).

Placed in the **AI Software Development** section beside reactor / vibe-monolith / risc. The evidence base is software-delivery-centric; the org widening keeps it from being narrowly dev-only but doesn't move it to Leadership.

Load-bearing evidence is the **peer-reviewed / first-party** studies (METR, BCG-HBS, Copilot RCTs, DORA); the AI-code debt figures are *corroborating colour*, attributed and hedged, never load-bearing — same discipline the reactor post used for cost percentages.
